stops.name: The Democratic Federation, crossing the river of fire
stops.campa: On the thirteenth of January, Morris, famous, prosperous, fifty years old, signs the membership card of the Democratic Federation and crosses what he calls the river of fire into revolutionary Socialism. He reads Marx, in French, and confesses he suffered agonies of confusion over the economics but grasped the wrong of it in his bones: that under this system the many toil in ugliness so that the few may waste in luxury. He gives his money, his fame and his failing strength to the Cause, and men who bought his wallpapers are scandalised to see him on soapboxes.
stops.quote: Apart from the desire to produce beautiful things, the leading passion of my life has been and is hatred of modern civilization.

stops.name: The Socialist League and Commonweal, lecturing in the rain
stops.campa: Splitting from Hyndman, Morris helps found the Socialist League and pours himself into its paper, Commonweal, which he edits and largely pays for. He tramps to open-air pitches on cold Sundays, dock-gates, street-corners, the moor at the edge of grim towns, and preaches Useful Work against Useless Toil to knots of working men, hoarse in the rain, heckled, sometimes arrested. He writes A Dream of John Ball, in which the priest of the 1381 rising speaks across five centuries: that men fight and lose the battle, and the thing they fought for comes about in spite of their defeat, under another name.
stops.quote: men fight and lose the battle, and the thing that they fought for comes about in spite of their defeat, and when it comes turns out not to be what they meant, and other men have to fight for what they meant under another name.
stops.quote_source: Morris, A Dream of John Ball (1888)

stops.name: Trafalgar Square, Bloody Sunday
stops.campa: On the thirteenth of November the unemployed and the Radicals march on Trafalgar Square in defiance of a police ban, and Morris marches with them. The horse and foot police charge; the crowd is clubbed and scattered; a working man named Alfred Linnell is ridden down and dies of his hurts. Morris walks in front of the vast funeral procession and writes the graveside song, A Death Song, sold to aid the dead man's children: not one man slain but many, killed by the great grey city that grinds the poor. The gentle dreamer of tapestries has learned what the State does to those who ask for bread.
stops.quote: Not one, not one, nor thousands must they slay, / But one and all if they would dusk the day.
stops.quote_source: Morris, 'A Death Song' for Alfred Linnell (1887)

stops.name: Kelmscott House, Hammersmith, News from Nowhere begins
stops.campa: From his Thames-side home at Hammersmith, Kelmscott House, named for the far manor at the river's other end, Morris launches in Commonweal, chapter by chapter from the eleventh of January, News from Nowhere. A man falls asleep in this grimed London and wakes into a green England after the Revolution: no money, no prisons, no factories, no masters; work become pleasure, the Houses of Parliament used to store manure, the Thames clean and salmon-full. It is his whole faith made into a country he can walk through, the utopia that answers all the others: not a machine-paradise but a return to joyful hand-work and fellowship.
stops.quote: Fellowship is heaven, and lack of fellowship is hell: fellowship is life, and lack of fellowship is death.
stops.quote_source: Morris, A Dream of John Ball (1888), the creed of his socialism

stops.name: Up the Thames to Kelmscott, the journey through the England-to-come
stops.campa: The dreamer rows up the summer Thames out of Nowhere's Hammersmith, past a cleansed and gardened London, through Runnymede and the locks, into the deep country, until the boat comes at last to the old grey many-gabled house among the elms: Kelmscott itself, the goal of the utopia, the heaven on earth set at the head of the river of time. There the vision fails and he is thrust back into his own harsh century; but he is bidden to go on living to make the dream true. Real England and the England-to-come meet at Kelmscott, and the whole atlas of utopias flows toward this one green door.
stops.quote: if others can see it as I have seen it, then it may be called a vision rather than a dream.
stops.quote_source: Morris, closing words of News from Nowhere (1890)

stops.name: The Kelmscott Press, the Golden type and the ideal book
stops.campa: In January, in a cottage by his Hammersmith house, Morris founds the Kelmscott Press to make the book a total work of art. He cuts his own types, first the Golden, drawn from the clear Roman of Jenson of Venice, then the Gothic Troy and Chaucer, grinds for the right black ink, hunts down handmade paper and vellum, and designs borders and initials thick as a garden. His aim, with his friend Emery Walker, is the ideal book: type, ink, paper, margin and ornament made one beautiful whole. The first book, his own Glittering Plain, comes off the press in the spring.
stops.quote: I began printing books with the hope of producing some which would have a definite claim to beauty... a book quite unornamented can look actually and positively beautiful.
stops.quote_source: Morris, 'A Note by William Morris on his Aims in Founding the Kelmscott Press' (1898)

stops.name: The Kelmscott Chaucer, a pocket cathedral
stops.campa: On the second of June the masterpiece is finished: the great folio Chaucer, four years in the making, with eighty-seven woodcuts after Burne-Jones's designs, fourteen huge borders and the ranked initials all from Morris's hand: the printed page become at last the illuminated manuscript's equal and heir. Burne-Jones calls it a pocket cathedral. The two old Oxford brothers, who dreamed at twenty of a Crusade against the age, hold the finished book together, both dying men now, and know the vow is kept. Of all the books of the machine age this is the one made wholly by the joy of the maker's hand.
stops.quote: when the book was done, if we live to finish it, it will be like a pocket cathedral — so full of design and I think Morris the greatest master of ornament in the world.
stops.quote_source: Edward Burne-Jones, on the Kelmscott Chaucer

stops.name: Kelmscott House, Hammersmith, the disease of being William Morris
stops.campa: Worn to nothing by twenty years of doing the work of ten men, he fails through the summer. A great physician, asked the disease, answers that it is simply being William Morris, and having done more work than most ten men. On the third of October, in his Thames-side house at Hammersmith, with the river he loved running past the window, he dies, aged sixty-two, murmuring that he wants to get the mumbo-jumbo out of the world. His doctor says plainly he died a victim of his enthusiasm for spreading the principles of Socialism. The dreamer of dreams, born out of his due time, is done.
stops.quote: I consider the case is this: the disease is simply being William Morris, and having done more work than most ten men.
stops.quote_source: Morris's physician, quoted in J. W. Mackail, The Life of William Morris (1899)

stops.name: Kelmscott churchyard, home to the river at the last
stops.campa: On a wild wet October day they bring him home up the Thames valley to Kelmscott, his heaven on earth. Not in a hearse but on a hay-wain, an open farm-cart wreathed in willow-boughs and vine, drawn by a farm-horse, the country funeral of a man who wished to be one of the country-folk who built his house. They lay him in the little churchyard of St George beneath a simple ridge-roofed stone that Philip Webb will design. The river runs on past the many-gabled house; the England-to-come he dreamed sails, in his book, forever up this water toward this door.
stops.quote: the many-gabled old house built by the simple country-folk of the long-past times.
stops.quote_source: Morris, News from Nowhere (1890), describing Kelmscott, the journey's end
